extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors / applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of written description, new-matter, and enablement issues under 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA and AIA), including how to assess claim amendments, genus/species support, range changes, and undue experimentation. Intended to direct examiner findings, burdens, and treatment of applicant replies and amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.' 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function, then the claim limitation is indefinite (35 U.S.C. 112(b)) and also lacks adequate written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) because an unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing the function and indicate lack of possession. See In re Donaldson Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner regarding written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry is case-by-case and a question of fact; description as filed is presumed adequate unless examiner rebuts presumption. Examiner has initial burden to present by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting, examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting lack of written description. Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a skilled person would not recognize possession of the claimed invention from the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. A simple statement pointing out lack of apparent support may be sufficient for new or amended claims where support is not apparent and applicant has not pointed it out. Suggest amendments when appropriate but avoid adding new matter. After applicant's reply, review the whole record (amendments, arguments, evidence); if record shows requirement satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If rejection is maintained, thoroughly analyze affidavits and reply evidence. See In re Wertheim; In re Marzocchi; Hyatt v. Dudas; Rasmussen; In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claim scope in original disclosure (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement and to be entitled to an earlier priority or filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle applies when claims are changed after filing (broadened, narrowed, numerical ranges altered, or terms changed). See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening by omission of a limitation (omission of essential feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification contains statements making a particular element the 'only possible location' or 'essential' or 'outside the purpose' to vary it, omission likely invalid (e.g., Gentry Gallery). If the specification does not describe a feature as essential, omission may be acceptable (e.g., In re Peters). A claim omitting matter disclosed to be essential may also be subject to enablement or indefiniteness rejections. See cases: Gentry Gallery; Tronzo; In re Wilder; In re Sus; In re Peters; In re Mayhew; In re Venezia; In re Collier; see also MPEP § 2172.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of a generic claim (genus supported by species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A written description for a claimed genus may be satisfied by sufficient description of a representative number of species; if substantial variation exists within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only one species supports a genus claim only if the disclosure indicates inventor possessed species sufficient to constitute the genus. When the art is unpredictable and ordinary artisans could not predict operability of other species, one species may not suffice (AbbVie v. Janssen; Enzo; In re Curtis). Conversely, in some circumstances a single species or functional recitation may adequately support a genus (Rasmussen; Herschler; Smythe). Disclosure teaching against other species can preclude genus support (Tronzo; In re Gosteli). Consider representativeness and predictability of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes (unsupported narrowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere 'laundry list' of moieties does not constitute written description support for every species. Adding a recited species not specifically disclosed can be improper (cases: Wattanasin; In re Ruschig; Rozbicki v. Chiang; Ex parte Ohshiro). Subgeneric terminology may be acceptable or not depending on whether reasonably communicated to skilled artisans; decide each case on facts (In re Lukach; Ex parte Sorenson; In re Smith; In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to numerical range limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical ranges, determine which ranges would be inherently supported by the original disclosure as understood by one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original range 25%-60% with examples 36% and 50%—a new claim 'at least 35%' failed because 'at least' had no upper limit and would cover embodiments outside 25%-60' (In re Wertheim); but 'between 35% and 60%' met description. Consider whether the specification indicates inventors considered particular ranges part of their invention (Purdue Pharma; Union Oil). Evaluate ranges in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description to new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of written description generally arises with respect to claim subject matter; amending abstract, specification, or drawings may introduce new matter if not described in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two statutory prohibitions on introducing new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no amendment introducing new matter into disclosure) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue). Information from one part of the application may be added to another part without introducing new matter, but additions beyond the original disclosure should be objected to or rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter by examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to claims, the examiner should reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification is amended to add new matter affecting claim limitations, a 112(a) rejection should be made. When amendments are filed in reply to objections/rejections, examine the entire application to determine whether new matter is involved; applicants should specifically point out support for amendments. The examiner should still consider the added subject matter for prior art rejections since new matter rejections may be overcome by applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and appealability of new matter objections/rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection of claims is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB); an objection/requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter and there is both a rejection and objection, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter present only in claims (antecedent and disclosure issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if the originally filed claims disclose material not elsewhere in the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification, use form paragraph 7.44. See In re Benno and MPEP § 608.01(o).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage that preserves the same meaning is permissible and does not constitute new matter; inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing may not be new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where multiple definitions exist, adding a definition must be clear from the application as filed that applicant intended that definition to avoid new matter or lack of written description problems. Example: substituting a more specific name for a term (Schering v. Amgen) may merely rename the invention and not add new matter if the original disclosure supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of obvious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a foreign priority document of record generally may not be relied upon to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. For inadvertent omission of portions in applications filed on/after Sept 21, 2004, 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.57 procedures apply. See In re Oda; Ex parte Bondiou; MPEP § 217.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function, theory, or advantage (doctrine of inherency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosing a device that inherently performs a function, has a property, operates by a theory, or has an advantage means the application discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not explicit; the application may later be amended to recite it without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must show the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. See In re Reynolds; In re Smythe; Yeda Research; In re Robertson; Kennecott.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may incorporate another document or part thereof by reference; the incorporated information is part of the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing the incorporated material with actual text is not new matter. See 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP § 608.01(p). Incorporation by reference affects determinations under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and 112(f). See MPEP § 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention defined by the claims so that one skilled in the art can make and use it; the invention to be enabled is that defined by the claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: ensure invention is communicated to the public meaningfully. It is not necessary to enable a perfected or commercially viable embodiment unless the claim requires it. Enablement is separate and distinct from written description; a limitation not described may nonetheless be enabling if one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention with that limitation. If claimed subject matter appears only in claims and not specification, object under form paragraph 7.44 for lacking support; treat enablement separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of enablement (undue experimentation standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard is whether one reasonably skilled in the art could make or use the invention from the disclosure together with knowledge in the art without undue experimentation (Minerals Separation/Hyde; In re Wands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent need not teach what is well known in the art. Any part of the specification (even background) can support enablement. Determination of enablement is a question of law based on factual findings. See In re Wands; United States v. Telectronics; In re Buchner; Hybritech; Lindemann Maschinenfabrik; Callicrate v. Wadsworth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for undue experimentation (Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when determining whether necessary experimentation is 'undue' include (but are not limited to): (A) breadth of the claims; (B) nature of the invention; (C) state of the prior art; (D) level of one of ordinary skill; (E) level of predictability in the art; (F) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) existence of working examples; and (H) quantity of experimentation needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are non-exclusive and must be considered together; it is improper to conclude non-enablement by analyzing only one factor while ignoring others. The examiner's analysis must consider all evidence related to each factor and base a conclusion on the evidence as a whole. See In re Wands; In re Wright; In re Certain Limited-Charge Cell Culture Microcarriers; cases illustrating application (Wands decision where specification provided considerable direction and art had high skill level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper basis for a conclusion of lack of enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion of lack of enablement means that, based on the evidence regarding the undue experimentation factors, the specification at filing would not have taught one skilled in the art how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must tie factual findings to legal conclusion; consider the totality of the evidence and not rely on speculation. See In re Wright; In re Wands; United States v. Telectronics.
